unit.title: Apply principles and practices in electrical installation

summary: This unit gives you the principles behind every installation job and the practices that make the work safe and neat. You will use Ohm's law, the power formula and energy in kilowatt-hours, work with series and parallel circuits, and learn how a Jamaican installation is supplied, protected and earthed. You will also choose cables and wiring systems, wire lighting and socket-outlet circuits, read layout drawings, make good terminations and test an installation dead before it is switched on.

blocks.p: Every installation job, from changing a light fitting to wiring a new house, rests on a few principles: how voltage, current and resistance are linked, how circuits are connected, and how cables, protective devices and earthing keep people and buildings safe. This unit teaches those principles and the everyday practices of good installation work. It is for Level 2 trainees who work under the supervision of a qualified electrician.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Work out current, voltage, resistance, power and energy with Ohm's law, the power formula and kWh, and explain series and parallel circuits.
Describe the supply and the installation
Explain how JPS supplies a building at 110 V and 220 V, and the job of the meter, main disconnect, distribution board and final circuits.
Explain why copper and PVC are used, read AWG sizes, and say what decides the size of a cable.
Install PVC conduit, boxes and accessories neatly, without overfilling the conduit, with joints only in boxes that can be reached.
Explain overload and short circuit, match a breaker to its cable, and explain earthing, bonding and GFCI protection.
Connect one-way, two-way and intermediate switching and socket outlets, with the switch in the line and the line to the lamp holder's centre contact.
Read layout drawings, circuit diagrams, symbols, legends, title blocks and scales, and use them to plan the work and list materials.
Strip without nicking, make tight terminations with no bare copper showing, and identify conductors at both ends.
Take part in the inspection and the dead tests (earth continuity, insulation resistance and polarity) and record the results.

ul: JPS supplies most homes and small businesses at **110 V and 220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**. Larger buildings may have a three-phase supply.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, so you will hear US terms (grounding, receptacle, panel, three-way switch) as well as British ones (earthing, socket outlet, distribution board, two-way switch). This kit gives both.
A new or altered installation must be inspected and certified by a licensed electrical inspector before JPS connects it. This is overseen by the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)**.
At Level 2 you work only under supervision, and you never work on a live circuit.

blocks.note: Before any work on an existing circuit, even changing a light fitting: switch off, lock off, tag, and prove dead with a tester that you prove works before and after the test. A wall switch is not an isolator.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Read the sections in order. Work every example yourself before reading the answer. Then try the practice test and read each explanation. Your instructor will show you the Centre's practice boards, tools and testers.
Everything in an installation is chosen to control four things: the push (voltage), the flow (current), what opposes the flow (resistance) and the rate at which energy is used (power).

head: Quantity
Symbol and unit
What it is
Measured with
rows: The flow of electrons round a circuit
An ammeter in series, or a clamp meter round one conductor
The push that drives the current round the circuit
A voltmeter across (in parallel with) the part or supply
An ohmmeter, with the circuit dead
The rate at which energy is used
Worked out from V and I, or read from the rating plate
Power used for a time: what JPS bills you for

blocks.p: Electrons are tiny charged particles in the atoms of a conductor. In copper many of them are free to move, and a voltage makes them drift round the circuit. (Diagrams show 'conventional current' flowing from + to −; the electrons themselves drift the other way. Both describe the same circuit.)

ul: **Material**: copper has a low resistance; steel more; PVC and rubber so much that they are insulators.
**Length**: a longer conductor has more resistance. Double the length, double the resistance.
**Thickness (cross-sectional area)**: a thicker conductor has less resistance. This is why heavy loads need bigger cables.
**Temperature**: copper's resistance rises as it gets hotter.

blocks.p: **V = I × R**, which can be rearranged as **I = V ÷ R** and **R = V ÷ I**. If the voltage stays the same and the resistance goes up, the current goes down; if the resistance goes down, the current goes up.

ul: A lamp takes 0.5 A from 12 V: R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = **24 Ω**.
3 A flows through a 4 Ω resistance: V = 3 × 4 = **12 V** across it.

blocks.note: Cover the quantity you want in the triangle V over I × R: V on top, I and R underneath. Covering V leaves I × R; covering I leaves V ÷ R; covering R leaves V ÷ I.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **P = V × I**, so **I = P ÷ V**. This is the formula you use most, because rating plates give the power. It is also true that P = I × I × R.

ul: A 1320 W microwave oven on 110 V: I = 1320 ÷ 110 = **12 A**.
A 4.4 kW water heater on 220 V: I = 4400 ÷ 220 = **20 A**.

The same appliance on a lower voltage draws less current but gives much less power. A 220 V heater wrongly put on 110 V gets half the voltage, draws half the current and gives only a quarter of its heat.

blocks.p: **Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (hours).** JPS bills by the kilowatt-hour.

ul: An air-conditioner drawing 1.2 kW for 8 hours a night uses 1.2 × 8 = 9.6 kWh a night, or 9.6 × 30 = 288 kWh in 30 nights.
At an example rate of J$70 per kWh, that is 288 × 70 = about J$20,000 a month. The real rate, with fuel and other charges, is on the JPS bill and changes from month to month.
A 10 W LED lamp left on for 10 hours uses only 0.1 kWh, about a sixth of the energy a 60 W filament lamp would use.

head: Effect
Where you meet it
rows: Elements in heaters, kettles and irons; fuses; the thermal trip in a breaker. It is also why an overloaded cable gets hot.
Motors, relays, contactors, transformers and the magnetic trip in a breaker
Charging batteries, electroplating, and corrosion where different metals meet
Electric shock: current through the body makes muscles clench and can stop the heart

blocks.p: **AC** (alternating current) changes direction many times a second. The JPS supply is AC at **50 Hz** (50 cycles a second). **DC** (direct current) flows one way only: batteries, solar panels and the inside of electronic equipment use it.
In a series circuit the parts are connected one after another, so there is only **one path** for the current.

ul: The **same current** flows through every part.
The supply voltage is **shared** between the parts: their voltages add up to the supply voltage.
The total resistance is the **sum** of the resistances: R = R1 + R2 + R3.
If one part fails open, the path is broken and **everything stops**.

blocks.p: **Example.** Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω in series on 12 V: R = 60 Ω, I = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.2 A. The voltages are 0.2 × 10 = 2 V, 0.2 × 20 = 4 V and 0.2 × 30 = 6 V, which add up to 12 V.
In an installation, things that must control or protect a load are in **series** with it: a switch, a fuse or breaker, a thermostat.
In a parallel circuit each part is connected across the supply on its own branch.

ul: Every branch gets the **full supply voltage**.
The total current is the **sum** of the branch currents.
The total resistance is **less than the smallest** branch. For two branches, R = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2); for equal branches, divide one value by the number of branches.
If one branch fails, the others **keep working**.

blocks.p: **Example.** 40 Ω and 10 Ω in parallel on 24 V: R = (40 × 10) ÷ (40 + 10) = 400 ÷ 50 = 8 Ω. The branch currents are 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 A and 24 ÷ 10 = 2.4 A, a total of 3 A, which is 24 ÷ 8.

blocks.h: Why buildings are wired in parallel

ul: Each lamp and appliance gets the full 110 V or 220 V that it is made for.
Each one can be switched on and off by itself.
A failed lamp does not put out the others.
But every load added to a circuit **adds current**, so the breaker and cable must be sized for the total.

blocks.p: **Example.** A 110 V bedroom circuit feeds four 15 W LED lamps (60 W), a 120 W television and a 60 W fan: 240 W in all, so I = 240 ÷ 110 ≈ 2.2 A.

A cable has a small resistance, and it is in **series** with the load. On a long run, some of the supply voltage is lost along the cable, so the load gets less than it should: lamps dim and motors struggle. Long runs and heavy loads therefore need thicker cables. A common design aim is to keep the drop on a final circuit within about 3% of the supply voltage.

blocks.note: A circuit where everything stops when one part fails is behaving as a series circuit. In a house, that points to a break in a shared conductor, such as a loose neutral at the first outlet on a run, not a fault in each appliance.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Follow the energy from the JPS line to the lamp, and you meet each part of an installation in turn.

flow: JPS transformer and line on the pole
Service drop (overhead) or service cable (underground) to the building
JPS meter: measures the energy used in kWh
Main disconnect (main breaker): switches off the whole installation
Distribution board (panel): breakers for each circuit, with neutral and earth bars
Final circuits: lighting, socket outlets and dedicated circuits
The loads: lamps, appliances and equipment

blocks.p: A typical house supply has **two line conductors and a neutral**. Each line is about 110 V to the neutral, and the two lines are about 220 V to each other. The neutral is connected to earth at the transformer and at the building's service. **Single-pole** breakers feed 110 V circuits from one line; **two-pole** breakers feed 220 V circuits from both lines and switch both together.

ul: **Busbars** carry the supply to the breakers.
The **neutral bar** collects the neutral conductors, and the **earth bar** collects the earth (grounding) conductors.
In the main panel at the service, and only there, the neutral and earth are joined by the **main bonding jumper**. In any sub-panel they are kept apart.
The **panel schedule** on the door lists what each breaker feeds. Keep it accurate.

head: Conductor
NEC colours (fixed wiring)
Colours you may meet on imported flexible cords
rows: Black, red or blue (any colour except white, grey or green)
Green, green with a yellow stripe, or bare copper

blocks.note: Follow the Centre's rules for colours, and never trust colours on old work: test to find out what each conductor is.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Lighting circuits**: often 15 A, feeding light points through switches.
**General socket-outlet circuits**: often 15 A or 20 A, feeding several outlets in parallel.
**Dedicated circuits**: one circuit for one large appliance, such as an air-conditioner, water heater, stove or pump, so that it cannot overload a shared circuit and can be isolated by itself.

head: Material
Why it is used
Notes
rows: Conducts very well, bends without breaking, is easy to terminate and resists corrosion
The usual conductor in building wiring
Used for larger service and feeder cables; needs terminals marked for aluminium (AL) and a larger size than copper for the same current
A good insulator; tough, cheap and does not rot
Cable insulation and sheaths, conduit, boxes; softens if overheated
A tough outer layer over thin PVC insulation
On THHN/THWN building wire, so it slides into conduit without damage

ul: **Conductor**: solid (one wire) or stranded (many fine wires, more flexible).
**Insulation**: on each conductor (core), to keep it apart from the others and from earth.
**Sheath**: an outer cover on multi-core cables that protects the insulated cores from damage, sun and damp. It does not carry a higher voltage; it protects.

head: Cable
Where it is used
rows: Pulled into conduit; very common in Jamaican concrete-block buildings
Dry places such as timber-framed walls and ceilings, fixed and protected as the code requires
Outdoor and underground runs, as the code allows
Connecting appliances and portable equipment; not for fixed wiring
Where the cable needs extra mechanical protection

blocks.p: In Jamaica conductor sizes are usually given in **AWG** (American Wire Gauge). **The smaller the number, the thicker the wire**: 10 AWG is thicker than 12 AWG, which is thicker than 14 AWG.

head: Copper size
Usual largest breaker
Typical use
rows: General outlets, kitchen and laundry circuits
Water heaters, dryers, smaller air-conditioners and ovens
About 40 A, or more where the code's temperature ratings allow

blocks.note: These are the usual limits for copper under the NEC. The electrician confirms every size from the code's tables, allowing for how and where the cable is installed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What decides the size of a cable

ul: **The current it must carry.** Add up the loads and use I = P ÷ V.
**How hot its surroundings are.** Roof spaces and conduit on sunny walls get very hot in Jamaica, and a hot cable can carry less current.
**How many cables are bunched together.** Many current-carrying conductors in one conduit cannot lose their heat as easily, so each must carry less.
**Voltage drop.** A long run may need a bigger cable so that the far end still gets enough voltage.
**The protective device.** The breaker must not be larger than the cable can safely carry.

head: System
Good points
Take care
rows: Does not rust; can be set into block walls and concrete slabs; light and easy to cut and join
It does not conduct, so a separate earth conductor must run in it. It expands in the sun: long outdoor runs need expansion fittings.
Rusts near the sea unless protected; joints must be sound if it forms part of the earth path.
For the final connection to motors, pumps and air-conditioners, which vibrate
Neat surface wiring where walls cannot be chased
Fit the lids and corner pieces properly.

blocks.p: Do not put too many cables in one conduit. An overfilled conduit traps heat, so the cables run hot, and the insulation can be scraped or torn as they are pulled in. The code limits fill: with three or more conductors they may take up no more than **40%** of the inside of the conduit. Use the fill tables to choose the conduit size, and if more conductors are needed, use a bigger conduit or a second run.

ul: **Device boxes** hold switches and outlets; **ceiling (octagon) boxes** hold light points; **junction boxes** hold joints.
Every joint must be made **inside a box or enclosure that can be reached later**, never buried in a wall or left in the middle of a conduit run.
Joints are made with **wire nuts** (twist-on connectors) of the right size, push-in connectors or terminal blocks. Never tape alone.
A **cable gland, bush or connector** where a cable or conduit enters a box protects the cable from the sharp edge and holds it firmly.
Outdoors, use **weatherproof** boxes and covers with their seals in place; outlets that may be used in the rain need covers that stay weatherproof with a plug in.
Close every unused knockout, and fit every cover.

head: Fault
What happens
What clears it
rows: Too much current for the circuit (too many appliances, or a struggling motor). The cable slowly overheats.
The breaker's thermal trip, after a delay that depends on the size of the overload
Line touches neutral (or another line) with almost no resistance between, so a very large current flows.
The breaker's magnetic trip, or a fuse, almost at once
Line touches earthed metal, such as a box or an appliance case.
The breaker, because the earth path lets a large current flow; a GFCI for small leakage currents

blocks.p: A **fuse** contains a wire that melts when too much current flows; it must be replaced with the same rating. A **circuit breaker** is a switch that trips open by itself and can be reset once the fault is found. Inside, a **bimetal strip** heated by the current trips it on overload (the heating effect), and a **coil** trips it instantly on a short circuit (the magnetic effect).

blocks.note: **The breaker protects the cable.** Its rating must be at least the current the circuit needs, but **no more than the cable can safely carry**. Then the breaker always trips before the cable overheats. Never fit a bigger breaker to stop a circuit tripping.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **GFCI** (ground-fault circuit interrupter, an RCD in British terms) compares the current going out on the line with the current coming back on the neutral. If about 5 mA is missing, leaking to earth, perhaps through a person, it trips in a fraction of a second. Breakers cannot do this: they need many amps to trip. GFCI protection is needed where people and water meet: bathrooms, kitchen counters, outdoors, garages, laundry areas and near sinks, as the code sets out.

ul: A GFCI outlet has **LINE** terminals for the supply and **LOAD** terminals that can protect outlets further along the circuit. Supply wired to the LOAD terminals by mistake leaves the outlet unprotected or unable to reset.
Test every GFCI with its TEST button when it is installed, and regularly after that.

flow: A ground rod (often copper-clad steel about 2.4 m long) is driven into the ground at the service
A grounding electrode conductor joins it to the earth bar in the main panel
The main bonding jumper joins the earth bar to the neutral, at the main panel only
An equipment grounding conductor runs with every circuit to every metal box, fitting and earth terminal

blocks.p: If a line conductor touches an earthed metal part, the fault current flows back through the equipment grounding conductor, which has a very low resistance. The current is large, so the breaker trips at once and the metal does not stay live. Without the earth conductor, the metal would stay live and the next person to touch it would get a shock. The connection to the ground rod also limits the voltages caused by lightning and by faults on the supply.

blocks.note: Never join neutral and earth anywhere except at the main panel. If they are joined at an outlet or a sub-panel, normal neutral current flows along earth conductors and metalwork, and GFCIs trip for no clear reason.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Bonding** joins metal parts that are not part of the electrical system, such as metal water pipes, gas pipes and structural steel, to the main earthing terminal. If a fault ever makes them live, they all stay at the same voltage and the breaker can trip; a person touching two of them at once does not get a shock between them. Earth and bonding connections must be tight, labelled and never removed.
One switch controls one or more lamps from one place.

head: Conductor
Goes from
Goes to
rows: The other terminal of the switch
The lamp holder's **outer screw shell** (straight, not through the switch)
The switch box, the switch's earth screw, the light fitting and every metal part

ul: The switch goes in the **line**, so that the lamp holder is **dead when the switch is off** and nobody changing a lamp is exposed to the supply.
The switched line goes to the **centre contact**, so that the outer shell, which fingers can touch when changing a lamp, is on the neutral.
A lamp lights whichever conductor is switched. So a switch wired in the neutral cannot be found by switching on: only a **polarity test** shows it.

blocks.p: Two switches control the same lamp from two places, such as the top and bottom of a staircase or the two ends of a passage. Each two-way switch has a **common** terminal and two **strapper** (traveller) terminals.

flow: Line from the breaker to the common terminal of switch A
Two strappers link the strapper terminals of switch A to those of switch B
The common terminal of switch B feeds the switched line to the lamp
The neutral goes straight to the lamp; the earth goes to every box and fitting

head: Switch A connects its common to
Switch B connects its common to
Lamp

blocks.p: Moving either switch changes which strapper carries the current, so the lamp changes from on to off, or off to on, from either place.

ul: On NEC-style switches the common terminal is usually a **darker** screw, and the strapper terminals lighter brass. Check the switch's own markings.
Strappers can be live, so they are never white, grey, green or bare. Use a line colour and mark them at both ends.

blocks.p: For three or more control points, **intermediate switches** go in the strappers **between** the two two-way switches. Each operation crosses the two strappers over, which changes the state of the lamp. Add one intermediate switch for each extra control point: a corridor with doors at both ends and two in the middle needs two two-way switches and two intermediates.

ul: 220 V outlets have a **different shape**, so that 110 V plugs cannot go in. Outlets for stoves and dryers that need both 110 V and 220 V also have a neutral.

Outlets on a circuit are connected in **parallel**. Join the earth conductors in each box with a short tail (pigtail) to the outlet's earth screw, so that taking one outlet out does not break the earth to the others.
Large loads get **dedicated circuits**: air-conditioners, water heaters, stoves, washing machines and pumps.
Mounting heights come from the drawing or the specification; keep them the same throughout a job.

head: Drawing
What it shows
rows: A plan of the building showing **where** each outlet, switch, light point, panel and circuit run goes
**How** the parts are connected, with symbols, but not where they are in the building
The actual connections, terminal by terminal, as the wires are run
Each breaker, its rating and what it feeds

flow: Read the title block: the job, the drawing number, the revision and its date, the scale, who drew and checked it
Make sure it is the latest revision
Read the legend, which explains every symbol on the drawing
Read the notes: mounting heights, cable sizes, special requirements
Follow each circuit: which switch controls which light, which points are on each circuit
Count the symbols and measure the runs to list the materials

blocks.note: **Standard symbols** let everyone read a drawing the same way. But symbols differ between US-style and British-style drawings, and between designers. Always use the drawing's own **legend**, and ask about any symbol it does not explain.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Circle with two short parallel lines through it
The same with 'GFCI' or 'GF' beside it
Circle (often with letters or a number)
Curved dashed line from a switch to lights
Line ending in an arrow, with a number
Home run: the cable back to the panel, with the circuit number

blocks.p: A scale tells you how many times bigger the real building is. At **1:50**, 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on the building; at **1:100**, 1 mm is 100 mm. Multiply the measured length by the scale number.

ul: At 1:100, a run of 37 mm on the drawing is 37 × 100 = 3700 mm = **3.7 m**.
At 1:50, a run of 64 mm on the drawing is 64 × 50 = 3200 mm = **3.2 m**.
Where the drawing gives a written dimension, use it instead of measuring.
Count each kind of symbol to list boxes, switches, outlets and fittings.
Measure each conduit and cable run, then add an allowance for drops to boxes, bends and terminations (often about 10–15%).
Note the circuits and the breaker sizes from the panel schedule.
Plan the order of work: boxes and conduit first, then cables, then terminations, then testing.
Mark changes made on site on the drawing (an 'as-built' copy), and report any part of the drawing that does not match the building before you start.
Mark out from the drawing with a tape measure and spirit level. Run conduit **straight, level or plumb**, never at odd angles, so that hidden runs can be found later.
Cut conduit square and **deburr** it inside and out, so that cables are not cut as they are pulled in.

Make bends smoothly with factory elbows, a bending spring (light conduit) or a heat gun or heating blanket (heavier PVC), with no kinks or flattening. Keep to no more than the equivalent of four right-angle bends between boxes.
Join PVC conduit with the right fittings and solvent cement.
Fix conduit with saddles at even spacing, within about 900 mm of each box and as the code and maker give along the run.
Fix boxes firmly, level, and flush with the finished wall.
Pull cables in with a fish tape, without forcing them, and leave at least about 150 mm of conductor in each box for terminating.

flow: Make sure the circuit is isolated and proved dead
Strip only the length the terminal needs (many devices have a strip gauge), using strippers set to the right size so the copper is not nicked
For a screw terminal, form a loop **clockwise**, the way the screw tightens; for a pillar or clamp terminal, push a straight end fully in
Tighten firmly, to the torque the maker gives where stated
Check that no bare copper shows outside the terminal and no insulation is trapped under the screw
Give the conductor a gentle pull to check that it is held

head: Poor termination
The danger
rows: Loose screw or loop pushed out
High resistance: the joint heats up, burns the accessory and can start a fire
Can be touched, or can touch another conductor: shock or short circuit
Less copper at the joint, so it runs hot
A weak point that can break or overheat
Conductors can slip out; copper can show below the nut

ul: **Identify** conductors at both ends (colour, sleeves or labels), so that each one can be traced and connected correctly, now and later.
Keep to one conductor under a screw unless the terminal is made for two.

blocks.h: Inspection and dead tests before switch-on

blocks.p: A new installation, or a new circuit, is **inspected and tested dead** before it is ever connected to the supply. A wrong connection or an earth fault could otherwise cause a shock, a fire or a flash the moment power is applied.

head: Check
How
Looking for
rows: A careful look at all the work against the drawing
Right cables and breakers, tight connections, no bare copper, covers fitted, conductors identified
Low-resistance ohmmeter from the main earth bar to every box, fitting and earth terminal
A low reading everywhere: every metal part is earthed
500 V DC between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth, with lamps and electronic equipment disconnected
High readings, at least the pass figure on the Centre's record sheet (often 1 MΩ)
Continuity checks with the circuit dead
Every switch in the line; the line to each lamp holder's centre contact; each outlet wired correctly

blocks.p: Only when all the dead tests pass does an authorised person (at the Centre, the instructor) connect the supply and switch on, with everyone standing clear. Then the live checks are made: the voltage at outlets, the GFCI test, and that every switch and light works. All results are recorded. A new installation is then certified by a licensed inspector before JPS connects it.

blocks.note: When you finish, clear off-cuts and dust, return tools, fit every cover, and leave the drawing marked with any changes. A tidy job is easier to inspect, safer to use and easier to maintain.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain current, voltage, resistance, power and energy, with their units.
I can use Ohm's law and P = V × I to work out current, voltage, resistance and power.
I can work out energy in kWh and an example cost in J$.
I can state the rules for series and parallel circuits and work out total resistance.
I can explain why buildings are wired in parallel and what voltage drop is.
I can describe the path of the supply from the JPS pole to the final circuits, and which loads use 110 V and 220 V.
I can give the NEC colours for line, neutral and earth.
I can explain why copper and PVC are used, read AWG sizes and say what decides a cable's size.
I can choose a wiring system and explain why conduit must not be overfilled.
I can explain overload, short circuit and earth fault, and match a breaker to a cable.
I can explain how earthing, bonding and GFCI protection keep people safe.
I can connect one-way, two-way and intermediate switching and explain how they work.
I can connect a socket outlet correctly.
I can read a layout drawing, its legend, title block and scale, and list materials from it.
I can install conduit, boxes and accessories neatly and make good terminations.
I can describe the inspection and dead tests before switch-on, and why they come first.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: The JPS supply to homes and small businesses
V = I × R; P = V × I; kWh = kW × hours
The three formulas you use most
Largest fill of a conduit with three or more conductors
Conductor left in a box for terminating
Common drawing scales: 1 mm = 50 mm, 1 mm = 100 mm
Insulation test voltage and a common pass figure

terms: Bonding
Joining metal pipes and structural metal to the main earthing terminal so that they stay at the same voltage.
Circuit breaker
A switch that trips by itself on overcurrent and can be reset.
Circuit diagram
A drawing that uses symbols to show how parts are connected, not where they are.
Conduit
A tube, often PVC, that cables run inside.
Dedicated circuit
A circuit that feeds one large appliance only.
Distribution board (panel)
The board that holds the breakers for the circuits.
Earthing (grounding)
Connecting exposed metal parts and the system to earth so that fault current has a safe path.
GFCI (RCD)
A device that trips when current leaks to earth, as through a person.
Intermediate switch
A switch fitted between two two-way switches so a lamp can be controlled from three or more places.
Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
A unit of energy: 1 kW used for 1 hour; what JPS bills for.
Layout drawing
A plan showing where the electrical points go in a building.
Legend
The key on a drawing that explains its symbols.
Load
The part of a circuit that uses the energy, such as a lamp or heater.
Ohm's law
V = I × R: current equals voltage divided by resistance.
Overload
More current than a circuit is designed to carry, for longer than it can stand.
Parallel circuit
A circuit in which each part is connected across the supply on its own branch.
Polarity test
A check that switches are in the line and that lamp holders and outlets are connected the right way.
Series circuit
A circuit with only one path, in which the same current flows through every part.
Short circuit
Line touching neutral (or another line) so that a very large current flows.
Strappers (travellers)
The conductors that link two-way switches.
Termination
Where a conductor is connected to a terminal.
Wire nut
A twist-on plastic cap with a spring inside, used to join conductors in a box.

c1.title: Reading the plan for a house in Bog Walk
c1.text: Trainee Akeela is helping Mr Clive Henry, an electrician, wire a new two-bedroom house in Bog Walk, St Catherine. The layout drawing is to a scale of 1:50, and its legend explains the symbols for outlets, switches, light points and the distribution board. On the drawing, the conduit run from the distribution board to the first bedroom outlet measures 86 mm. The title block shows 'Revision B', but the copy in the van is 'Revision A'. One symbol near the back door is not in the legend.

c2.title: Corridor lighting at a Runaway Bay hotel
c2.text: At a small hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, a long corridor has a door at each end and one in the middle. The owner wants the corridor lights to be switched on and off at all three doors. Trainee Garfield is wiring it with his supervisor, Miss Annette Morris. They will use two two-way switches (called three-way switches in NEC terms) and one intermediate switch (a four-way switch).

c3.title: Cook shop circuits in Port Antonio
c3.text: Miss Simone Walters is opening a cook shop in Port Antonio, Portland. On one 110 V counter circuit she wants to run a 1500 W kettle, a 1000 W sandwich toaster and a 300 W blender at the same time. A separate 220 V circuit will feed a 5500 W oven. The counter circuit is wired in 12 AWG copper with a 20 A breaker. Trainee Romario is helping Mr Keith Bryan, the electrician, check the plans.

c4.title: Tests before switch-on in Highgate
c4.text: Trainees have wired a small barber shop in Highgate, St Mary. Before anything is switched on, Mr Lorenzo Campbell's team inspects and tests the installation dead. They find: (1) a lamp holder with its centre contact on the neutral and its switch in the neutral; (2) an insulation resistance reading of 0.05 MΩ between line and earth on circuit 3; (3) a metal switch box with no earth conductor connected to it.

c5.title: First terminations in Black River
c5.text: Trainee Sasha is fitting outlets and switches in a community centre in Black River, St Elizabeth, under supervision. Her supervisor finds a conductor looped anticlockwise round a terminal screw, and another with three strands cut off so that it would fit its terminal. Sasha also plans to pull eight 12 AWG conductors into a conduit that the fill table allows to hold only five of that size.

questions.q: About what real length does the 86 mm run on the drawing stand for?
questions.why: At 1:50, 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on the building: 86 × 50 = 4300 mm = 4.3 m. Dividing by 50 (1.72) is a common slip. Add extra for the drops to the boxes and for terminations when you order cable.

questions.q: What should Akeela do about the two revisions of the drawing?
o: Use both, taking whichever is easier in each room
Work from Revision B and set Revision A aside
Use Revision A, since it is the copy in the van
Wait until the job ends, then compare the two
questions.why: A later revision replaces the earlier one: outlets or circuits may have moved. Work only from the latest issue, take the old copy out of use, and ask the supervisor if you are not sure which is current.

questions.q: What should she do about the symbol that is not in the legend?
o: Ask Mr Henry or the designer what it means
Leave that point out of the materials list
Guess from the nearest symbol that looks like it
Fit an ordinary outlet, the most common point
questions.why: Symbols vary between drawings, and between US and British practice, so the legend is the key. A symbol it does not explain must be checked with the supervisor or the designer before materials are ordered or the work starts.

questions.q: Where does the intermediate switch go in this circuit?
o: Between the distribution board and the first switch
Between the last switch and the lamps, in the neutral
Across the lamps, between line and neutral
Between the two two-way switches, on the strappers
questions.why: The intermediate switch sits in the strappers between the two two-way switches. Each operation crosses the strappers over, so the lamps change state from any of the three doors. More intermediate switches can be added for more control points.

questions.q: Which conductor connects to the common terminal of the two-way switch at the far end of the run?
o: One of the strappers from the middle switch
The switched line to the lamps
The line from the corridor's breaker
The neutral from the distribution board
questions.why: The line goes to the common of the first two-way switch, the strappers link the switches, and the common of the last switch sends the switched line to the lamps. The neutral goes straight to the lamps and never through a switch.

questions.q: Which colours could Garfield use for the strappers in this NEC-style installation?
o: Green, as they only link two switches together
Red or blue, marked as strappers at both ends
Bare copper, as they are inside the conduit
White or grey, as they are not the line conductor
questions.why: Strappers can be live, so they must not be white or grey (kept for the neutral) or green or bare (kept for the earth). A line colour such as red or blue, marked at both ends, tells the next electrician what they are.

questions.q: On each two-way (three-way) switch, which terminal is usually the darker-coloured screw?
o: One strapper terminal
The earth terminal
The common terminal
The neutral terminal
questions.why: On NEC-style three-way switches the common terminal is usually dark (black or bronze) and the two strapper (traveller) terminals are lighter brass; the earth screw is green. Always check the switch's own markings, as makers differ.

questions.q: About what current would the counter circuit carry with all three appliances running?
o: About 280 A
About 13 A
About 25 A
About 2.5 A
questions.why: Add the powers: 1500 + 1000 + 300 = 2800 W. Then I = P ÷ V = 2800 ÷ 110 ≈ 25 A. 13 A would be the current on 220 V, but this circuit is 110 V.

questions.q: What is the right advice about the counter circuit?
o: Keep it as it is, since breakers take time to trip
Fit a 30 A breaker, since the cable can take the extra heat
Split the loads over two circuits; keep the 20 A breaker
Change to 14 AWG cable, which is easier to pull in
questions.why: About 25 A is more than a 20 A breaker and 12 AWG cable are meant for. A bigger breaker would let the cable overheat. Spread the appliances over two or more circuits so that each carries a safe current.

questions.q: Which cable and breaker suit the 5500 W oven circuit?
o: 10 AWG copper on a 30 A two-pole breaker
14 AWG copper on a 30 A two-pole breaker
12 AWG copper on a 40 A two-pole breaker
10 AWG copper on a 50 A single-pole breaker
questions.why: 5500 ÷ 220 = 25 A. 10 AWG copper is normally protected at up to 30 A, and a 220 V circuit needs a two-pole breaker that switches both lines. 14 AWG and 12 AWG are too small for 30 A or 40 A, and a single-pole breaker leaves one line live. Mr Bryan confirms the size from the code tables.

questions.q: Miss Walters uses the 1500 W kettle for 2 hours a day for 30 days. At an example rate of J$70 per kWh, about what does that cost?
questions.why: Energy = power in kW × hours: 1.5 kW × 2 h × 30 = 90 kWh. Cost = 90 × J$70 = J$6,300. J$210 is only one day, and J$630 slips a decimal point. Real JPS bills add other charges, so check the rate on the bill.

questions.q: Why could finding (1) not have been found just by switching the lamp on?
o: The lamp would light only when the switch is off
The breaker trips at once whenever the lamp is on
The lamp works normally either way round
The lamp would not light at all with this fault
questions.why: A lamp lights whether the switch breaks the line or the neutral, so a function test hides the fault. Only a polarity test shows that the holder stays live when the switch is off, which is why it is done dead, before switch-on.

questions.q: What is a likely cause of the 0.05 MΩ reading on circuit 3?
o: A core damaged by a screw, nail or stripping
A switch left in the off position during the test
Too many outlets connected to the one circuit
A breaker that is too small for that circuit
questions.why: A very low reading between line and earth means the insulation is broken somewhere: often a core nicked when stripping, a cable pierced by a screw or nail, or insulation crushed at a box edge. Find and repair it before the circuit is switched on.

questions.q: Which dead test should have found finding (3)?
o: Polarity of the switches and lamp holders
Measuring the supply voltage at the board
Insulation resistance between line and the neutral
Continuity of the protective (earth) conductors
questions.why: The continuity test of the protective conductors checks that every box, fitting and earth terminal is joined to the main earth with a low resistance. An unearthed metal box could become live in a fault and stay live without tripping the breaker.

questions.q: Why is the anticlockwise loop a problem?
o: The current then flows the wrong way round the screw
It makes the conductor carry less current
It reverses the polarity of the outlet
Tightening the screw pushes the loop outwards
questions.why: A screw turns clockwise to tighten. A loop formed clockwise is drawn in under the head; an anticlockwise loop is pushed out, leaving a loose joint that runs hot. Form the loop clockwise, or use a straight end in a pillar or clamp terminal.

questions.q: Why is cutting off strands to make a conductor fit wrong?
o: The joint has less copper, so it can overheat
It changes the conductor's size on the drawing
It lets the conductor carry more current safely
It is fine as long as the screw is very tight
questions.why: The conductor was sized to carry the circuit current. Cutting strands reduces the copper at the terminal, so that point runs hot and can burn the accessory. Use a terminal that suits the conductor, or the right size of conductor.

questions.q: What should Sasha do about the conduit?
o: Pull them in with plenty of cable lubricant
Use a larger conduit, or run a second one
Use thinner conductors so that all eight fit
Pull in the eight, then check them for heat
questions.why: An overfilled conduit lets cables run hot, because the heat cannot escape, and the insulation can be damaged as they are pulled in. Lubricant only eases pulling; it does not make more room. Choose a conduit size the fill table allows, or split the circuits.

questions.q: A 60 Ω resistor and a 30 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. What is the total resistance, and what current does the supply give?
o: 45 Ω and 0.27 A
90 Ω and 0.13 A
30 Ω and 0.4 A
20 Ω and 0.6 A
questions.why: For two in parallel, R = (60 × 30) ÷ (60 + 30) = 1800 ÷ 90 = 20 Ω, less than the smaller resistor, as it must be. I = 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 A, which is the sum of the branch currents, 0.2 A and 0.4 A.

questions.q: Three identical lamps are connected in series across a 110 V supply. About what voltage is across each lamp?
o: About 37 V
About 55 V
questions.why: In series the supply voltage is shared. Three identical lamps share 110 V equally, 110 ÷ 3 ≈ 37 V each, so they glow dimly. In parallel, each would get the full 110 V.

questions.q: A circuit breaker's thermal trip works by which effect of current?
o: Chemical action, which eats a link
Light, which falls on a sensor
Heating, which bends a bimetal strip
Magnetism, which pulls in an iron plunger
questions.why: The thermal trip uses the heating effect: overload current warms a bimetal strip until it bends and trips the breaker, after a delay. The magnetic trip uses the magnetic effect of a large fault current to trip it almost at once.
